> A NeoPixel clock that has NeoPixels around it to tell the time and an OLED display to show the current date, with a switch to change modes. It retrieves the date and time using the XIAO ESP32-C3 to get it using Wi-Fi. I will use MicroPython for the code.

### 2026-11-07: For this session, I was mainly swapping parts to fit within the budget, but I also placed the OLED pin headers on the PCB, which I did first.

**2.98h**

For this session, I was mainly swapping parts to fit within the budget, but I also placed the OLED pin headers on the PCB, which I did first.

I used AI to try to find the exact dimensions the headers should be relative to the silkscreen, but then I realized that it didn't have to be placed exactly on the silkscreen.

After that, I had to try and find parts that cost less to fit the BOM's budget, because when I got the price of the PCB from JLCPCB, I realized that it cost more than I thought it would and I would have to swap out some parts. I swapped out the XIAO ESP32C3 for the ESP32C3 Super Mini since it was cheaper on AliExpress. Then I swapped the 2.42" OLED for the same OLED I used for Week 4 since it was cheaper and I didn't have to find another part. Even that wasn't enough, so I chose the most expensive thing on my BOM after that other than the PCB, which was the pack of resistors from AliExpress. I tried many options as a replacement, but the shipping or the unit price made it too expensive. I thought I was going to have to settle for 2 ~$2.50 packs for each resistor value and probably have to cut the price on another part, which would be very difficult since all of them past that were < $5, but then AI found gold with a ~$2.50 pack of 300 which included both resistor values and more, and the shipping cost was free. I just hope it isn't a scam.

[Timelapse](https://lookout.hackclub.com/api/media/5db3fa08-81ff-4d7c-801a-edb09b811a59/video.mp4)

### 2026-11-08: First, I had to replace the PCB with the new components. This was fairly simple as I just had to place the components similarly to how I had done before.

**2.47h**

First, I had to replace the PCB with the new components. This was fairly simple as I just had to place the components similarly to how I had done before.

Second, I had to rewire the PCB. The components had changed position, so I had to rewire them because of that. During this, however, I realized that I forgot to add the 680uF capacitor on the 5v to the LED's, so I had to add it and place it. I also kept switching back and forth between which side I wanted to put the components on. Now I realize that I will need to put the ESP32-C3 Supermini on the bottom so the USB C cable doesn't get in front of any LED's.

Third, I made an assembly in Onshape for the PCB. I exported the PCB from EasyEDA and downloaded a model of the Supermini from GrabCAD. I tried to make the PCB into an assembly so it was easier to update, but that wasn't working very well.

[Timelapse](https://lookout.hackclub.com/api/media/5a167e3b-7a5f-40b6-9f8c-16e8b212a660/video.mp4)

### 2026-11-08: # Finishing PCB and Assemblies

**2.23h**

# Finishing PCB and Assemblies

In this session, I finished the PCB, finished the PCB assembly in Onshape, and I added a full assembly with all of the parts. Then, in addition to the timelapse, I added holes to zip tie the cable to the PCB to hold it in place if I choose to use them. And for the second, shorter timelapse, I moved the Supermini so the USB C cable wouldn't interfere with the PCB.

## First timelapse

- First, I finished the PCB by moving the Supermini to the other side and adding the mounting holes. I had to move the Supermini to the other side so the cable didn't get in the way of the LED's. I was debating whether or not to move the other components to the other side (except the OLED obviously), but I chose not to because the 680uF capacitor wouldn't fit without a larger standoff and because I thought it added to the look of the PCB.
- Second, I finished the PCB assembly in Onshape with the newly finished PCB. The copper pads for the Supermini were now on the other side, and when I tried to extrude the copper pads so I could select them, it wouldn't work. I then had to insert almost all of the copper surfaces on the bottom side and fasten them so they would work. Then I fastened the Supermini to it. Then I imported the OLED and fastened that to the PCB.
- Third, I made a full assembly with all of the parts. I imported the OLED stabilizer part I made in Week 4 since I was using the same display and also the M2x10mm standoffs that I downloaded from GrabCAD. Then I inserted those and the PCB Assembly into the full assembly.

## In between timelapses

- After that, I realized that I might want to keep the cable in place on the back of the PCB. The cable is designed to go up the back of the PCB and plug into the USB C port on the ESP32-C3 Supermini. I made two holes so a zip tie could loop through them and hold the cable in place.

The holes:

### 2026-11-10: In this session, I continued to work on the code, making the actual Date and Time Test AND...

**0.1h**

In this session, I continued to work on the code, making the actual Date and Time Test AND...

First, I made the Date and Time Test. I copied some of the code over from the main program, but I had to make a  lot of it myself, like the getDate and getTime functions, and the function to retrieve whether or not it is DST. Then I went through a cycle of debugging with AI, fixing the problems, debugging, fixing, and so on.

After I verified that that was working, I moved on to the main program. I first copied the functions from Date and Time Test into the main program so I could use them, and then I worked on the main loop. I first worked out how reconnecting to wifi and retrieving the time would work to handle exceptions. Then I moved on to the NeoPixels. When I started on this, I realized that what I thought was smart by putting led 1 to the right where minute 1 on the clock goes was actually not since the index starts from 0. I was going to fix it in the PCB, but it wouldn't load. Then I just made the code to set the values for the leds for the hour, minute, and second, and made a function to make a trail behind them.

### 2026-11-10: ## First Timelapse

**4.03h**

## First Timelapse
First, I had to add the switch to change the modes since I forgot about it before and it is necessary. I added it in the schematic and updated the PCB with the switch I found that was within budget. Then I updated the assembly, having to redo all of the board in the PCB Assembly.

After that, I updated the PCB files in the repo, and then I made the README to meet the requirements, with the images and links to whatever I felt like linking to.

## Second Timelapse
Then I realized that I would need a keycap to go onto the switch, so I made it in Onshape based off of the model of the switch. I then downloaded the files for the keycap and assemblies and put them in the repo. Then I just updated the README and called it a day.

## Third Timelapse
I'm getting tired of this: I fix a problem that needs a timelapse, move onto the code, and then find another problem I have to fix with a timelapse. This time it was to fix the LED placement on the PCB. I saw it in my TODO I made in my code. I had to move the LED's over, redo the nets, and reupload the files to the repo.

## Extra 45 mins
After I fixed the LEDs, I realized that I had forgot to rename them. I tried to rename them all together, but that didn't work, so I had to do it manually.

Finally, I decided to make ticks for my clock so time was easier to tell. I made silkscreen lines to do this.

### 2026-11-11: ## Fixing lines

**0.33h**

## Fixing lines
For 20 minutes, I was fixing the lines in the PCB since I realized they didn't need to be as long as they were. I shortened them to either 0.125 or 0.25 inches long from where the LED ends, depending on if it was in 3, 6, 9, and 12 or if it was another hour number on the clock.

## Code
I first had to refactor the code to include the switch. I made a switch test program with a function to check the status of the switch, accounting for debouncing and copied that code into the main program.

Then I made the code for the trail of a dim red color for the fractions of a second (it goes around one time for each second), I made code to get the decimal for the fraction and then to convert that into which LED is supposed to light up. Then I set that LED and made the trail behind it. I also changed the values for the other LEDs, realizing that they were too bright before.

After that, I made the code for the OLED to get the date and print it to the screen. This was fairly simple to get the date and print it out, centered on the screen, but I did have to figure out how to format it to the amount of digits (either 2 or 4 depending on which part it was).

Once I finished that, I checked with AI to make sure everything would work properly in theory, and it's a good thing I did. I found numerous errors with almost everything. I had to clear and write the neopixels, move the initial wifi call, add the condition for the mode, change the hour led, add the UTC offset change code in the loop, and change the centerText function.
